articles.title: Word Count and Line Count: Why Every Tool Disagrees
articles.excerpt: You paste a draft into one tool and it says 1,204 words. Your editor says 1,198. A colleague runs wc -w and gets 1,211. Nobody made a mistake: each tool is answering a slightly different question, and…
articles.body: You paste a draft into one tool and it says 1,204 words. Your editor says 1,198. A colleague runs wc -w and gets 1,211. Nobody made a mistake: each tool is answering a slightly different question, and none of them tells you which one. The fix is knowing what each count actually measures. If you just want the numbers, the Skojio word counter shows words, characters, lines and bytes side by side, and explains which is which. A "word" is a definition, not a fact: hyphens, dashes, emoji and CJK text are where tools disagree. wc -l counts newline characters, so it is often one off from the line numbers your editor shows. One emoji can be 1 character, 2 code points, 4 UTF-16 units or 8 bytes, depending on who is counting.

articles.title: A payment that never unlocked the plan: what our own webhook got wrong
articles.excerpt: Someone paid for our product and got nothing. The payment went through, the provider sent us the event, and our handler answered with a success code. The customer was charged and their account stayed…
articles.body: Someone paid for our product and got nothing. The payment went through, the provider sent us the event, and our handler answered with a success code. The customer was charged and their account stayed on the free plan. Nobody got an error, so nobody noticed. Here is what happened, and the three checks we added so it cannot happen silently again. The payer had no account yet The customer paid before they created an account. Our webhook looked up the account by the payer's email, found nothing, and returned 200 . From the provider's side the delivery succeeded, so it never retried. const user = await findUserByEmail ( email ) ; if ( ! user ) { logger . warn ( "no registered user, skipping" ) ; return NextResponse . json ( { received : true } , { status : 200 } ) ; } That 200 is the bug.

articles.title: CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md: what happens with conflicting information? Is there a precedence order?
articles.excerpt: Claude Code has no precedence order for conflicting CLAUDE.md instructions; Codex and Cursor do. Here is what each tool loads, which file wins, and how to remove the conflict instead of hoping the rig…
articles.body: Claude Code has no precedence order for conflicting CLAUDE.md instructions; Codex and Cursor do. Here is what each tool loads, which file wins, and how to remove the conflict instead of hoping the right file wins. Originally published on clogmeter.vercel.app . In Claude Code there is no precedence order: every CLAUDE.md it finds is concatenated into context, nothing overrides anything, and Anthropic's docs say that if two instructions contradict each other "Claude may pick one arbitrarily." Codex and Cursor do define a winner (the closest AGENTS.md for Codex; Team → Project → User rules for Cursor), but in every tool that ordering is a hint to the model, not a guarantee. The only reliable fix is to keep each rule in exactly one place.

A field gets removed by an upgrade, a module is uninstalled, or an expression meets a record with an empty value, and the template breaks. Disclosure: I make a paid Odoo module that tests templates (link at the bottom). The technique below works without it. I tried it on Odoo 19: _generate_template with a broken placeholder in email_to returns an empty recipient and no error. The email just has nobody to go to. Calling _render_field on the same field raises the real error.

articles.title: A Day Isn't 24 Hours: Fixing Date Math & DST Bugs
articles.excerpt: TL;DR: Adding 24 hours to a timestamp does not reliably move a clock forward by one calendar day. Because of Daylight Saving Time transitions, a calendar day can span 23, 24, or 25 hours. To prevent b…
articles.body: TL;DR: Adding 24 hours to a timestamp does not reliably move a clock forward by one calendar day. Because of Daylight Saving Time transitions, a calendar day can span 23, 24, or 25 hours. To prevent brittle tests and production bugs, always perform date math using calendar intervals rather than fixed durations of hours or seconds. There is nothing quite as humbling as watching an entire CI pipeline turn red on code nobody has touched in months. A test suite runs cleanly for weeks, pull requests merge without incident, and then—out of nowhere on a random Sunday night—builds start failing across unrelated branches. When code breaks without anyone modifying it, the culprit is almost always an external assumption leaking into your test suite.

articles.body: Published State AI Laws Are Moving Faster Than Federal AI Regulation AI regulation in the United States has an unusual source: individual states. While federal policymakers debate how artificial intelligence should be governed, state legislatures have already begun writing laws that affect hiring software, automated decision systems, consumer privacy, transparency, and algorithmic accountability. For developers, product leaders, and compliance teams, this creates a complicated environment. The legal requirements may vary by state, making implementation harder. But waiting for a single federal framework also has a cost. By the time national legislation arrives, companies may have already shipped products and built compliance processes around state-specific rules.

articles.title: SpaceX moves Starship Flight 15 booster to launch pad for 'squeeze test' ahead of epic double-catch attempt (photos)
articles.excerpt: SpaceX has moved its Starship Super Heavy booster to the pad to prep for the next test flight of the megarocket, a historic mission scheduled to launch this Friday (Nov. 13).
articles.body: SpaceX is one big step closer to the 15th test flight of its Starship megarocket. The company announced today (Nov. 10) that it had moved its latest Starship first stage, known as Super Heavy Booster 22, to the launch mount at its Starbase facility in South Texas ahead of Flight 15, which is scheduled to lift off this Friday (Nov. 13). During the upcoming launch test, SpaceX plans to catch both Booster 22 and Starship's Ship upper stage with its launch tower's "chopstick" arms in a double landing catch — something the private spaceflight company has never tried before. It will be the first full recovery of an orbital rocket in history. SpaceX's Flight 15 Starship Super Heavy booster in its assembly bay, before its move to Starbase's launch mount.

articles.title: Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose, and John Leguizamo reveal why they joined Andy Weir's sci-fi audio drama 'Exoplanet' (interview)
articles.excerpt: We hooked up with Mackie, DeBose, and Lequizamo to learn more about this renaissance of audio dramas and what attracted them to board Weir's sci-fi thriller.
articles.body: In any respectable audiobook project, finding the names of Andy Weir ("The Martian," "Project Hail Mary") and Benjamin Percy ("The Ninth Metal," "Wolverine") attached would elicit intense fan interest, but add the superstar vocal talents of Anthony Mackie ("Avengers: Infinity War," "Avengers: Doomsday"), Ariana DeBose ("West Side Story"), and John Leguizamo ("Ice Age"), and it catapults this sonic odyssey into the stratosphere. Such is the case with " Exoplanet ," Audible Original’s new 7-episode science fiction audio drama executive produced by Weir and penned by Percy. Its planet-hopping space disaster narrative sees the crew of the starship Wild Blue Yonder hit a quantum anomaly, forcing their ship to crash-land onto a deadly exoplanet.

articles.title: Microsoft Fixes Nearly 1,100 Security Vulnerabilities
articles.excerpt: Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month's Patch Tuesday ad…
articles.body: Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe , Apple , Google and Mozilla . Image: Shutterstock.com. Diorama by @zepp1969. November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 10, 2013: Europe's GOCE satellite, the 'Ferrari of space,' fell out of orbit after mapping Earth's gravity field
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 10, 2013, Europe's GOCE satellite fell to Earth after four years in orbit mapping the planet's gravitational field. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 10, 2013, Europe's GOCE satellite fell to Earth after four years in orbit mapping the planet's gravitational field. GOCE, its name was short for Gravity field and steady-state Ocean Circulation Explorer, launched in 2009 on a mission to map Earth's gravity like never before. But despite that successful mission, it was doomed in 2013 when it ran out of fuel . At the time, controllers weren't sure where GOCE would fall back to Earth . Some people worried that it might crash into a populated area. However, the small spacecraft broke up in the atmosphere and didn't cause any property damage. It disintegrated about 50 miles above the Falkland Islands in the South Atlantic Ocean. The European Space Agency called the mission a success. GOCE lasted far longer than expected.

articles.title: Grok Build coding agent leaks oodles of confidential info, some belonging to SpaceXSI
articles.excerpt: Researcher finds 35,000 Grok Build apps wide open to anyone who looked for them.
articles.body: Grok Build, the vibe-coding agent from SpaceXSI, is leaking data—some of it proprietary business information and other sensitive secrets—from thousands of its users, including the very same Elon Musk-owned company that offers the platform, new research shows. The information is revealed through links allowing Grok Build users to share their apps with others. Grok takes steps to randomize the URLs so only people who know the exact URL can access the data stored there. A design decision by developers of the platform, however, completely torpedoes that objective and makes it possible for anyone to enumerate thousands of live Grok Build projects. Except in rare cases, clicking those links opens the app and reveals all data associated with it.
